summary.value: This paper introduces a new cross-tokenizer ensemble approach. The method constructs a mapping matrix that aligns one tokenizer’s vocabulary to another (base) vocabulary using prefix relations. In addition, the authors propose an entropy-based weighting scheme to combine ensemble outputs adaptively. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements over previous methods.

strengths.value:
While the method is largely heuristic, its reported performance appears reasonable and may be of some practical interest. The use of tokenizer priors is a sensible design choice and appears more effective in practice compared to earlier methods such as Unite and DeepEN.

The experimental evaluation is sufficiently thorough to support the authors’ main claims.

The proposed method is more efficient than prior works such as DeepEN.

weaknesses.value:
The token-translation method is mainly heuristics and is not theoretically grounded compared to other approach, for example the character-ensemble baseline converts the every model to the same base character alphabet with statistical guarantees.

For cross-tokenizer problem, it is necessary to include the amount of overlapping tokens between the vocabularies. For example, Llama3 and Qwen2.5 shares a large amount of similar tokens.

The idea of using entropy for model combination is not new (see [1], for example). It would be important to include a comparison against other methods with entropy-weighted ensembles. In particular, Table 2 could include a separate row showing the proposed approach without entropy weighting (i.e., “ToT without entropy weighting”) to clarify its contribution.


[1] Ruan, Yangjun, et al. "Weighted Ensemble Self-Supervised Learning." The Eleventh International Conference on Learning Representations.

comment.value:
Dear Reviewer TweT,

Thank you for your valuable feedback, which has helped us improve the clarity and quality of our paper. We have incorporated the corresponding revisions into the updated manuscript, where all revisions and additions are highlighted in blue for your convenience. We detail our responses below, and please kindly let us know if our replies address your concerns.

> **W1.** The token-translation method is mainly heuristics and is not theoretically grounded compared to other approach.  

Thank you for the question. Although Token Translation is simple to implement and requires no tuning after a single one-time mapping, **it is not a heuristic method**. To clarify, we present a formal justification showing that ToT implements a **deterministic form of causal alignment** between heterogeneous token probability spaces. Under standard assumptions satisfied by modern BPE and Unigram tokenizers, ToT produces a **deterministic causal mapping** of the conditional probabilities involved in cross-model alignment. This provides a clear **theoretical foundation**.

Let $\mathcal{V}\_{\text{assist}}$ and $\mathcal{V}\_{\text{main}}$ denote the vocabularies of the assist and main models, respectively. We posit a shared, continuous ground-truth text space $\mathcal{S}$ representing all possible raw text strings. The objective of token alignment is to project the probability mass from an assist token $v^{(\text{assist})} \in \mathcal{V}\_{\text{assist}}$ to a target main token $v^{(\text{main})} \in \mathcal{V}\_{\text{main}}$.

The true conditional probability is:

$$
P(v^{(\text{main})} \mid v^{(\text{assist})})=
\sum\_{s \in \mathcal{S}}
\underbrace{P(v^{(\text{main})} \mid s)}\_{\text{Main Prior}} \cdot
\underbrace{P(s \mid v^{(\text{assist})})}\_{\text{Assist Decoding}}
\tag{1}
$$

To make the above tractable, we introduce two assumptions satisfied by modern BPE/Unigram tokenizers:

- **Assumption 1 (Deterministic Decoding).**  
  A token $v^{(\text{assist})}$ maps deterministically to a unique textual form string. That is, $P(s \mid v^{(\text{assist})})$ follows a Dirac delta distribution:

  $$
  P(s \mid v^{(\text{assist})}) 
  = \mathbb{1}[s = Tok\_{\text{assist}}.\mathrm{decode}(v^{(\text{assist})}) \]
  $$

- **Assumption 2 (Canonical Encoding Prior).**  
  Given any string $s$, the main model’s tokenizer deterministically produces a unique canonical tokenization:

  $$Tok\_{\text{main}}.\mathrm{encode}(s) = [t\_1, t\_2, \dots]$$

  Because autoregressive models generate text in a causal left-to-right manner, any generation of $s$ must begin with its first token $t\_1$. Accordingly, in our alignment derivation we use the indicator:

  $$\mathbb{1}[v^{(\text{main})} = t\_1]$$

  which reflects the deterministic **tokenization mapping**, rather than any assumption about the determinism of the model’s next-token **probability distribution**.


Under these assumptions, the intractable sum in Eq. (1) collapses into a single indicator function, which serves as our Ground Truth Causal Alignment:

$$
P\_{\text{true}}(v^{(\text{main})} \mid v^{(\text{assist})})=
\mathbb{1}\left[
v^{(\text{main})}=
\mathrm{First}\left(
Tok\_{\text{main}}.\mathrm{encode}(Tok\_{\text{assist}}.\mathrm{decode}(v^{(\text{assist})}))
\right)\right]
$$

Our ToT method computes exactly this alignment via the forward translation matrix $M^{(\text{pre})}$:

$$
\hat{P}\_{\text{ToT}}(v^{(\text{main})} \mid v^{(\text{assist})})
\triangleq
M^{(\text{pre})}\_{v^{(\text{assist})}, v^{(\text{main})}}
$$

By construction:

$$
M^{(\text{pre})}\_{i,j} = 1
\quad\text{iff}\quad
j = \mathrm{First}(Tok\_{\text{main}}.\mathrm{encode}(Tok\_{\text{assist}}.\mathrm{decode}(i)))
$$

Thus:

$$
\mathbb{E}[\hat{P}\_{\text{ToT}}] = P\_{\text{true}}
$$

This proves that ToT is a **deterministic causal mapping** (and, in deterministic tokenizers, an exact calculator) of the underlying causal conditional probability.


Consider the case where a single assist token expands to a multi-token main sequence $[t\_1, t\_2, \dots, t\_n]$.

Let:

- $E\_{\text{seq}}$ = the event that the main model generates the full sequence  
- $E\_{t\_1}$ = the event that it generates $t\_1$

Since:

$$
E\_{\text{seq}} \subseteq E\_{t\_1}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
P(E\_{\text{seq}}) \le P(E\_{t\_1})
$$

If the assist model predicts $v^{(\text{assist})}$ with probability $p$, then the main model must assign at least probability $p$ to $t\_1$, because $t\_1$ is the **necessary causal precursor** of the full token sequence.

Therefore assigning:

$$
\hat{P}(t\_1) \leftarrow p
$$

faithfully preserves probability mass and yields a **deterministic causal mapping** for next-token prediction.

The performance of the prefix alone is already impressive and surpasses the baselines, as shown in Table 3 in the paper. Furthermore, through back translation, $M^{(\text{sup})}$ complements the probability mass, allowing the ensemble to better capture the representation of the underlying sequence.

To evaluate whether other uncertainty measures could be competitive, we implemented several alternatives, all defined on the full probability distribution for fairness and consistency. These include **full-distribution entropy**, **distribution variance**, **calibration-based confidence using 1−max(p)**, and a **main–assist disagreement score** based on the KL divergence between the two models’ predicted distributions. In the disagreement-based version, **strong divergence** between main and assist decreases the assist’s weight, while **agreement increases it**. We replaced only the uncertainty scoring function and kept the routing framework identical across all methods. Empirically, **top-k entropy achieves the highest average performance (32.30)**, while the full-distribution measures and the disagreement-based score yield slightly lower results. | **Top-k Entropy (Ours)**               | Entropy over normalized top-k mass             | **32.30**      |

These results clarify the contribution of entropy weighting and highlight that the proposed **top-k formulation provides strong overall performance**.

summary.value: This paper proposes a simple, lightweight, and training-free model ensembling method called Token Translation (ToT). Instead of relying on computationally expensive or semantically weak alignment methods (like embedding similarity or string heuristics), ToT leverages the "tokenizer priors", i.e., the statistical segmentation behavior learned by each model's tokenizer. Extensive experiments demonstrates the effects of this method.

strengths.value:
S1: The authors propose a simple yet highly effective training-free ensembling method that aligns the vocabularies of different models using only tokenization rules, presenting substantial practical potential.

S2: The authors conduct comprehensive experimental evaluations, demonstrating the effectiveness and broad applicability (and ease of use) of the proposed method.

weaknesses.value:
1. The authors propose a simple, direct, and effective training-free model ensembling method. However, because the method relies only on the token priors and lacks additional supervision, it is susceptible to potential biases. The paper would benefit from more extensive ablation studies and analyses to demonstrate the method’s generality and robustness.

2. The proposed ToT method is asymmetric. The authors should therefore include a series of experiments that swap the roles of the main model and the assistant model, demonstrating that the method's effectiveness is not contingent on a particular model assignment.

3. The authors should expand empirical validation along several axes, for example: accuracy w.r.t. the number of ensemble members (extending beyond Figure 2); cross-family evaluations (e.g., Llama, Gemma, Qwen, GLM, GPT-OSS, etc.); different model architectures (dense models versus MoE models); and different model scales (e.g., 32B dense models or larger MoE models).

4. Given that many open-source models now share similar tokenizers, the authors should consider evaluating ensembles that include models with more divergent tokenizers to verify that the proposed technique holds when tokenizer differences are larger.

5. Because the method requires only token logits or log-probabilities, it can be applied together with closed-source models. To strengthen the broad applicability of the method and provide additional insights, the authors may attempt ensembles incorporating closed-source models (e.g., using OpenAI GPT‑4/5 API). Even if such combinations do not yield large gains, reporting these results would be valuable for follow-up work.

6. The mapping matrix derived from rule-based procedures primarily encodes tokenization priors and is therefore weakly context-aware. To increase the method’s practical credibility, the authors should present a more detailed and intuitive analysis of the mapping matrix: examine the token priors it captures, investigate underlying mechanisms such as token conflicts and cooperation, and provide theoretical discussion plus focused case studies that illustrate the behavior and limitations of the mapping matrix.

questions.value:
Q1: The method intuitively works better when ensembling models of similar scale. Could the authors attempt to extend the approach to ensembles that combine small and large LMs (i.e., cross-scale ensembles, beyond the scale of RQ4) to see whether it can meaningfully raise the overall performance ceiling? Demonstrating effectiveness in the small-LM vs. large-LM setting would substantially increase the practical value of the work.

Q2: Since this family of methods seems to be particularly effective for base/instruction-tuned models, the authors might also investigate its effects on reasoning models — specifically in Chain-of-Thought scenarios. Such an analysis (e.g., whether the method changes reasoning trajectories) would help clarify the mechanism and impact of the approach on multi-step reasoning.

> **W1.** No formal analysis of when/why token translation produces valid alignments. Why is the first re-encoded token the right choice? What properties ensure coherence? 

Thank you for the question. To clarify, we provide a rigorous theoretical justification for our Token Translation (ToT) framework. We demonstrate that ToT is not a heuristic approximation, but rather a deterministic implementation of *Exact Causal Alignment* between heterogeneous probability spaces. Specifically, we show that our method yields a **deterministic causal mapping** of the conditional probabilities required for cross-model alignment under standard tokenizer assumptions.


Let $\mathcal{V}\_{\text{assist}}$ and $\mathcal{V}\_{\text{main}}$ denote the vocabularies of the assist and main models, respectively. We posit a shared, continuous ground-truth text space $\mathcal{S}$ representing all possible raw text strings. The objective of token alignment is to project the probability mass from an assist token $v^{(\text{assist})} \in \mathcal{V}\_{\text{assist}}$ to a target main token $v^{(\text{main})} \in \mathcal{V}\_{\text{main}}$.

The true conditional probability is:

$$
P(v^{(\text{main})} \mid v^{(\text{assist})})=
\sum\_{s \in \mathcal{S}}
\underbrace{P(v^{(\text{main})} \mid s)}\_{\text{Main Prior}} \cdot
\underbrace{P(s \mid v^{(\text{assist})})}\_{\text{Assist Decoding}}
\tag{1}
$$

To make the above tractable, we introduce two assumptions satisfied by modern BPE/Unigram tokenizers:

- **Assumption 1 (Deterministic Decoding).**  
  A token $v^{(\text{assist})}$ maps deterministically to a unique raw textual form string. That is, $P(s \mid v^{(\text{assist})})$ follows a Dirac delta distribution:

  $$
  P(s \mid v^{(\text{assist})}) 
  = \mathbb{1}[s = Tok\_{\text{assist}}.\mathrm{decode}(v^{(\text{assist})}) \]
  $$

- **Assumption 2 (Canonical Encoding Prior).**  
  Given any string $s$, the main model’s tokenizer deterministically produces a unique canonical tokenization:

  $$Tok\_{\text{main}}.\mathrm{encode}(s) = [t\_1, t\_2, \dots]$$

  Because autoregressive models generate text in a causal left-to-right manner, any generation of $s$ must begin with its first token $t\_1$. Accordingly, in our alignment derivation we use the indicator:

  $$\mathbb{1}[v^{(\text{main})} = t\_1]$$

  which reflects the deterministic **tokenization mapping**, rather than any assumption about the determinism of the model’s next-token **probability distribution**.


Under these assumptions, the intractable sum in Eq. (1) collapses into a single indicator function, which serves as our Ground Truth Causal Alignment:

$$
P\_{\text{true}}(v^{(\text{main})} \mid v^{(\text{assist})})=
\mathbb{1}\left[
v^{(\text{main})}=
\mathrm{First}\left(
Tok\_{\text{main}}.\mathrm{encode}(Tok\_{\text{assist}}.\mathrm{decode}(v^{(\text{assist})}))
\right)\right]
$$

Our ToT method computes exactly this alignment via the forward translation matrix $M^{(\text{pre})}$:

$$
\hat{P}\_{\text{ToT}}(v^{(\text{main})} \mid v^{(\text{assist})})
\triangleq
M^{(\text{pre})}\_{v^{(\text{assist})}, v^{(\text{main})}}
$$

By construction:

$$
M^{(\text{pre})}\_{i,j} = 1
\quad\text{iff}\quad
j = \mathrm{First}(Tok\_{\text{main}}.\mathrm{encode}(Tok\_{\text{assist}}.\mathrm{decode}(i)))
$$

Thus:

$$
\mathbb{E}[\hat{P}\_{\text{ToT}}] = P\_{\text{true}}
$$

This proves that ToT is a **deterministic causal mapping** (and, in deterministic tokenizers, an exact calculator) of the underlying causal conditional probability.


Consider the case where a single assist token expands to a multi-token main sequence $[t\_1, t\_2, \dots, t\_n]$.

Let:

- $E\_{\text{seq}}$ = the event that the main model generates the full sequence  
- $E\_{t\_1}$ = the event that it generates $t\_1$

Since:

$$
E\_{\text{seq}} \subseteq E\_{t\_1}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
P(E\_{\text{seq}}) \le P(E\_{t\_1})
$$

If the assist model predicts $v^{(\text{assist})}$ with probability $p$, then the main model must assign at least probability $p$ to $t\_1$, because $t\_1$ is the **necessary causal precursor** of the full token sequence.

Therefore assigning:

$$
\hat{P}(t\_1) \leftarrow p
$$

faithfully preserves probability mass and yields a **deterministic causal mapping** for next-token prediction.

The performance of the prefix alone is already impressive and surpasses the baselines, as shown in Table 3 in the paper. Furthermore, through back translation, $M^{(\text{sup})}$ complements the probability mass, allowing the ensemble to better capture the representation of the underlying sequence.

> **W2&Q3.** When does token translation fail? Can you characterize failure patterns?  


Thank you for the question. In our analysis, there are **two primary sources of failure: token alignment limitations and the capability of the assist model itself.**

First, token translation can break down in **extreme cases where the two tokenizers belong to completely different linguistic systems.** For example, English vs. Japanese subword vocabularies share almost no prefixes, morphology, or compositional structure. In such scenarios, forward and backward mappings become extremely sparse. However, these situations are rare in practice, as most model pairs used in modern LLM ensembles are trained on overlapping multilingual corpora and retain substantial tokenizer compatibility.

Second, failure can arise from the **model’s inherent knowledge or capacity limitations.** For example, on NQ, the Gemma-2-9B-IT model attains only 13.49 accuracy as a standalone model. When a model is weak on a specific task, even uncertainty weighting cannot fully suppress its influence, and the ensemble may degrade. **This reflects a model-capability constraint rather than a failure of the alignment mechanism itself.**


---

> **W3.** No principled guidance for setting hyperparameters for new model pairs or explanation of whether optimal values vary by task, model combination, or language. Ablations show robustness over ranges but don't justify the chosen defaults or explain when to deviate.


Thank you for the question. One of the advantages of Token Translation is that **it requires no model- or task-specific tuning.** Across all model pairs and all benchmarks in the paper, we use **exactly the same default hyperparameters and the same alignment matrix**, generated once and reused throughout. This consistency already yields strong performance, indicating that ToT provides a **stable cross-model interface** that does not require adaptation for each new setting.

We choose the defaults (e.g., ($\alpha$=0.5) and top-(50) uncertainty) because **our ablations show that performance remains stable across a broad range of values** (see Figures 3–5 in the appendix), with no sharp optima or task-dependent modes. These settings balance the main and complementary mappings while providing a stable uncertainty signal that avoids unnecessary noise. **In practice, we observe no need to deviate from these defaults** when adding new model combinations or tasks.



---

> **W4.** Why is entropy over top-k the right measure versus alternatives (variance, disagreement, calibration)?


Thank you for raising this point. Our choice of **entropy over the top-k tokens** is motivated by the observation that, for modern LLMs, the candidate next token almost always resides within the top-k portion of the distribution. **The tail beyond top-k contains probabilities dominated by noise**, and including them often inflates uncertainty estimates without adding meaningful information. Focusing on the top-k region therefore provides a **more faithful and elegant view of the model’s effective uncertainty.**

To evaluate whether other uncertainty measures could be competitive, we implemented several alternatives, all defined on the full probability distribution for fairness and consistency. These include full-distribution entropy, distribution variance, calibration-based confidence using 1−max(p), and a main–assist disagreement score based on the KL divergence between the two models’ predicted distributions. In the disagreement-based version, **strong divergence between main and assist decreases the assist’s weight**, while agreement increases it. We replaced only the uncertainty scoring function and kept the routing framework identical across all methods. **Empirically, top-k entropy achieves the highest average performance (32.30)**, while the full-distribution measures and the disagreement-based score yield slightly lower results. The comparison is summarized in the table below.


| Uncertainty Measure                    | How It Works                                   | Avg. Score (↑) |
|----------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|----------------|
| Entropy              | Entropy over full vocabulary distribution      | 32.13          |
| Variance             | Variance over distribution                | 31.10          |
| Calibration (1 − max prob)             | Confidence proxy using max probability         | 31.56          |
| Disagreement          | KL(main \| assist); large gap → lower assist   | 31.28          |
| **Top-k Entropy (Ours)**               | **Entropy over top-k mass**             | **32.30**      |

These results clarify the contribution of entropy weighting and highlight that **the proposed top-k formulation provides the competitive overall performance.**

Thank you for the question. Token Translation produces valid alignments under two formal assumptions we introduced before, both of which are satisfied by standard BPE and Unigram tokenizers.  
(1) **Deterministic decoding:** each token corresponds to a unique raw text string.  
(2) **Canonical encoding:** for any string (s), the tokenizer produces a unique, deterministic segmentation where the first token is the causal precursor required for autoregressive generation.

These assumptions ensure that encoding yields a **valid causal alignment of next-token probabilities**.

Importantly, alignment quality is *not* determined by vocabulary overlap or training corpus similarity. What matters is the **segmentation strategy** imposed by the tokenizer: two tokenizers produce compatible alignments when their segmentation rules reflect **similar subword decomposition patterns**. Because these segmentation rules capture the **causal structure** used by autoregressive LLMs, they naturally support token-level fusion and allow ToT to remain effective across diverse model pairs.




---

> **Q4.** You show 2-4 models which is sufficient, but what happens with 10+ models? Is there diminishing returns or computational bottlenecks?  

Thank you for the suggestion. Adding more assist models increases computational cost, while the overall performance gain tends to be limited. To assess this, **we combined all seven available models** (Gemma 9B, GLM 9B, InternLM 7B, LLaMA 8B, Mistral 7B, Qwen 7B, Yi 9B) using ToT, with **LLaMA 8B as the main model**. The resulting **7-model ensemble reached 74.92 on TriviaQA**, which is slightly higher than the 2-model and 4-model ensembles. This indicates that ToT can still benefit from additional diversity, but **the improvements become smaller** as more models with varying strengths are added.




---

> **Q5.** Given the minimal ablation impact, is uncertainty-aware weighting actually essential or could you achieve similar results with simpler uniform weighting plus alignment?  

Thank you for the question. While **uniform weighting + token translation** already provides strong performance, the **uncertainty-aware weighting becomes particularly important** in settings where the two models differ substantially in capability or where the assist model may introduce noisy signals. In knowledge-gap scenarios, such as when one model is much weaker on a given task, the uncertainty term helps **down-weight unreliable predictions** and prevents degradation. It can also be useful in multiple-choice question answering benchmarks where token alignment (multiple choice A, B, C etc. in ARC-c dataset) is straightforward and the main challenge lies in **suppressing overconfident but incorrect logits** from the weaker model. In these cases, **uncertainty-aware weighting contributes clear and consistent improvements** over uniform averaging.

---

We hope our responses adequately address your concerns, and we would be happy to discuss anything further if needed.**

This paper proposes token translation to address tokenizer mismatch in test-time LLM, which aligns heterogeneous token spaces by decoding tokens from a source tokenizer and re-encoding with a target tokenizer.
